Mr. Chair, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. I am very pleased to join you after a long and productive week to congratulate you on the successful conclusion of this session. As I indicated in my opening remarks on Monday, I came into this week with an open mind, ready to listen, to engage, and to learn. Throughout the week, I have met with many delegations and participants, and I'm happy to say that at the end of the 35th session, I am very encouraged and inspired by the level of commitment and engagement witnessed throughout these past 5 days. We had over 1,500 participants joining us this week, 126 member states represented, and several high-level ministers and deputy ministers. This speaks to the enduring value and importance of this Commission as the principal policymaking body of the United Nations in the field of crime prevention and criminal justice. Through your discussions and decisions, you have helped shape the international response to some of the most pressing challenges of our time, while also laying a strong foundation for the upcoming Crime Congress in the United Arab Emirates. I look forward to carrying the momentum and outcomes of this session into that important gathering later in the year. This platform continues to provide a unique and irreplaceable space where dialogue can continue, trust can be built, and collective solutions forged together. That spirit was evident in the work you undertook this week. You negotiated and adopted by consensus 3 important resolutions addressing timely, highly relevant, and contemporary issues. As someone who has spent some time of my professional life around negotiating tables, I know firsthand that multilateral progress is rarely linear. Negotiations move slowly, word by word, sentence by sentence, paragraph by paragraph. At times, it can feel as though we take one step forward only to take two steps back. Yet the history of multilateralism, and indeed the history of these commissions, was not built overnight. It was built over time through patience, persistence, and perseverance, and it was built by people like yourselves who are willing to stay at the table. To continue the conversation and to search for common ground even when differences remained and which at times may have seemed insurmountable. That is the essence of multilateralism and of diplomacy, and it is that essence that we must continue to nurture and to preserve, because the impact of our work here does not end when this conference hall empties. It endures in the laws that we shape, the communities we help protect, and the people whose lives are ultimately improved by the decisions we take. This session was also enriched by more than 100 side events covering a remarkable range of real-world issues, from cybercrime and online scams to human trafficking, access to justice, prison reform, and many other pressing topics. I had the pleasure of attending one of these events with the head of the Presidential Administration of Uzbekistan on empowering women and youth for more resilient societies. These side events are incredibly valuable and an important fixture of these commissions as they connect the theoretical with practical real-world experience. The same spirit of partnership was evident in the strong participation by civil society. More than 600 representatives from 135 NGOs joined us this week, and I had an enriching and engaging dialogue with them. They bring unique perspectives and insight that ensure we do not lose sight of the people we are here to serve. It is the contribution of these diverse actors and stakeholders that shows how effective multilateralism is in bringing people together around a common goal to solve common challenges. Ladies and gentlemen, I like to end every meeting and event on a positive note, so before you leave today, I would like to take this opportunity to once again thank all the colleagues working behind the scenes who made this session possible. In particular, I wish to thank Jo and her team as the Secretariat of the Commission, our interpreters and translators, security personnel, conference management services, and the many staff members across UNODC, UNOAV, and UN Information Service, and my own office, who have put their all into this week and contributed to the smooth running and success of this session. I would also like to convey special gratitude to Ambassador Bond for his leadership as Chair of the Commission. Every orchestra needs a conductor, and you have conducted these proceedings with professionalism and calm pragmatism. A special mention also goes to Ambassador Kaifu of Japan for navigating the proceedings of the Committee of the Whole with diplomatic prowess and grace. I hope you all take with you a renewed appreciation of the value of dialogue and renewed confidence in what we can achieve when we work together. Only when we work together can we contribute to a safer, better protected, dignified, and prosperous humanity. I wish you all a safe journey home, and a restful weekend after 5 days of hard work. I thank you very much and good evening.
